structure.title: Books I–III · A child learns what the grown-ups admire
structure.text: Augustine prays to God as he remembers learning language, fearing the schoolmaster and discovering the attractions of the theatre. The older speaker can now hear the adult approval that helped teach the boy which desires counted as respectable.

structure.title: Books IV–VII · An educated man changes his mind
structure.text: Friendship, loss, teaching and travel accompany an increasingly difficult search for truth. In Milan, the bishop's preaching and philosophical reading loosen intellectual objections to Christianity before the question of how Augustine wants to live has been settled.

structure.title: Books VIII–IX · Other lives make a claim on this one
structure.text: Stories about people who have changed their lives press on someone who can already explain why he should change. Conversion, baptism and conversations with his mother bring the remembered life to a natural stopping place, although the book has much farther to go.

structure.title: Books X–XIII · The man praying now
structure.text: Memory and present temptations replace the sequence of past events. Reading Genesis leads Augustine to ask what it could mean for creation to begin when time itself belongs to what was created. The prayer to God continues across the change of subject.

people.name: Monica
people.role: A mother praying alongside the story
people.text: Her hopes for her son's salvation accompany his travel and professional ambitions. Augustine remembers both the concrete arrangements a mother could make and the changes she could only continue to ask for.

people.name: Ambrose
people.role: The bishop Augustine first hears as a professional
people.text: Trained in public speaking, Augustine has reasons to listen to a celebrated preacher before he is ready to believe him. Attention to a speaker's manner gradually admits the possibility of hearing something in his meaning.

people.name: The divided will
people.role: A person able to argue both sides alone
people.text: Augustine can want a changed life and still want the old one to last a little longer. The difficulty survives the correction of an intellectual error because the person who would issue the command is also the person resisting it.

context.title: An autobiography addressed to God
context.text: The human reader overhears an address to someone Augustine believes already knows everything. Telling the truth here has purposes other than supplying information, including praise and acknowledging what the speaker owes.

notice.text: Stay with the stolen pears after the theft.
notice.why: The pears were poor and the boys had better fruit. Augustine keeps subtracting plausible motives until the companions and the pleasure of the forbidden act come into much sharper focus.

notice.text: Listen when a text reaches somebody through a voice.
notice.why: A sermon, a remembered story, a child's song and a scriptural passage reach listeners at particular moments. The words acquire consequences partly through the life already being lived by the person who hears them.

opening: Augustine wants a different life, but he would prefer to keep the pleasures of this one a little longer. He has explanations for the delay, intellectual questions to resolve, and ambitions that make conversion inconvenient. Writing to God, he revisits the child who stole, the young man who wanted admiration, and the adult who could recognise an evasion while continuing to rely on it. The intimacy comes from a mind refusing to let its eventual transformation tidy away the embarrassment of how long it resisted.
